What if you could turn the same material into a conductor, insulator, magnet, or even a superconductor just by twisting it? Meet magic angle graphene, where a tiny 1.1° twist creates a
items.why_watch: The video centers on a real materials science phenomenon where the same substance can be flipped between conductor, insulator, and magnet depending on how it's structured — a discovery with huge implications for computing and energy. Be Smart does its usual job of grounding abstract physics in tangible stakes, and the 'Science Across America' framing surfaces researchers you won't find in the standard science media circuit. Worth it if you follow materials science or just want a well-reported dispatch from a working lab.

items.title: The One Principle That Explains All Physics - But Why?
items.description:
Thanks to Brilliant for sponsoring this video! Try everything Brilliant has to offer at https://brilliant.org/PhysicsExplained — and get 20% off an annual premium subscription.

The Action Principle lies at the heart of modern physics, from mechanics to electromagnetism, relativity, and the Standard Model. In this video, we explore why a simple thrown ball follows one particular path out of infinitely many, and how this reveals a deeper rule: the physical path is the one that makes the action st
items.why_watch: This video makes a serious attempt to explain the Principle of Least Action — the single mathematical idea underlying classical mechanics, electromagnetism, relativity, and quantum field theory — not just as a calculational trick but as a conceptual puzzle worth sitting with. Physics Explained doesn't shy away from the real question of why nature seems to 'minimize' anything at all, which is more philosophically honest than most physics explainers. Best watched with a pen nearby if you want to follow the math, though it's accessible without it.

items.title: I never understood Black Body Radiation - Until Now!
items.description:
Head to https://squarespace.com/floatheadphysics to save 10% off your first purchase of a website or domain using code FLOATHEADPHYSICS

This video was animated by Talha
Instagram: reelengine
gmail: reelenginestudios@gmail.com

Let's explore why black body radiation was one of the most puzzling concepts of the 1900s. And in this series, we will see how it eventually led Max Planck to the quantum revolution!

Chatpers:
00:00 Intro
02:02 We are all glowing!
04:04 Why can't we 'see' the glow? 
05:2
items.why_watch: FloatHeadPhysics reconstructs the specific conceptual crisis that blackbody radiation posed to classical physics — namely, why hot objects glow the colors they do, and why every 19th-century explanation catastrophically failed. The animation makes the ultraviolet catastrophe genuinely intuitive rather than just named, and the video frames it as the first domino that forced Planck, reluctantly, to invent quantum theory. A clean 18 minutes that earns its place as a quantum mechanics origin story.

items.title: What does asbestos do to a person?
items.description:
How asbestos ended up everywhere, and why we’re still using it today. Sponsored by Ground News - Go to https://ground.news/Ve for 40% off the unlimited Vantage plan, to catch how major public health stories are covered across the political spectrum and spot media bias for yourself.

If you’re looking for a molecular modelling kit, try Snatoms, a kit I invented where the atoms snap together magnetically - https://ve42.co/SnatomsV 

Sign up for the Veritasium newsletter for weekly science updates
items.why_watch: Veritasium goes deep on how asbestos became embedded in so much of the built world, and — the genuinely unsettling part — why it's still being mined and used today despite what we know. The video traces the industrial, regulatory, and lobbying history that kept it in production, which turns out to be as much a story about institutional failure as it is about chemistry. At nearly an hour it's thorough, but the pacing earns the length.

items.title: Anthropologist Answers Evolution Questions
items.description: Anthropologist Agustín Fuentes joins WIRED to answer the internet's burning questions about human evolution. Are humans still evolving? Was there a first human? What does the family tree leading to humans look like? Is monogamy in human relationships natural or something society imposes? Did early people really live in caves? Who invented kissing? Were the Neanderthals stronger than us? Why didn't other human-like species survive? Answers to these questions and many more await on Human Evolution
items.why_watch: Agustín Fuentes tackles genuinely tricky questions — like whether there was literally a 'first human' and whether monogamy is biologically wired or culturally constructed — with the precision of someone who actually studies this for a living. The Q&A format keeps it moving, and he's refreshingly willing to complicate the tidy stories most of us absorbed in school. Good for anyone who wants evolution explained without the usual pop-science shortcuts.

items.why_watch: Max Miller digs into the specific rations and field cooking of Italian WWII soldiers, a perspective that rarely gets covered compared to American or German counterparts. The contrast between official military nutrition policy and what soldiers actually ate reveals a lot about Italy's fraught relationship with the war itself. As always, Miller recreates a period recipe, so there's a hands-on anchor to the history.

items.title: THG Podcast: Counterfactuals - A Churchill and Roosevelt Christmas, 1941
items.channel_title: The History Guy: History Deserves to Be Remembered
items.description:
Listen to this episode of the THG Podcast, which posts in addition to regular History Guy content, after it releases on podcast services. Subscribe to the RSS feed for more: https://www.spreaker.com/show/6153862/episodes/feed

Note: We are continuing to upload older audio podcasts that haven't been put on YouTube. As we did not record video for these they are audio-only. Video podcasts upload with each new podcasts every other week.

Today we talk about a little remembered battle that could have
items.why_watch: This counterfactual episode asks what might have unfolded differently if Churchill and Roosevelt's famous Christmas 1941 meeting — just weeks after Pearl Harbor — had gone another way, when the entire Allied strategy was still being shaped. The History Guy uses the format not for idle speculation but to highlight how contingent the actual decisions were, and how much hinged on the personal dynamic between two very particular men. Audio-only, but well-suited to a long walk or commute.

items.title: Cello - In Search of a Voice - Kate Kennedy
items.description:
0:00 // Introduction — a cellist, her shadow and what an instrument really means
3:26 // The journey — following six cellos and their players across Europe
7:24 // The Cristiani Stradivarius — the first female cello soloist and her forgotten Siberian odyssey
11:05 // Cremona — the treasure trove and playing a cello that bears the scars of its adventures
14:55 // The Mendelssohn — how a composer wrote a cellist's voice into his music
17:18 // The Mara Stradivarius — surviving the Nazi occupation
items.why_watch: Musicologist Kate Kennedy traces six specific cellos across Europe, including a Stradivarius owned by the first female cello soloist — a woman whose story ended in a forgotten Siberian exile. This is less a lecture about music theory and more a piece of detective history, following instruments that outlived their players and carry the physical marks of their journeys. If you've ever thought about what an object accumulates over centuries of use, this one will stay with you.

items.why_watch: This is a practical week-four walkthrough of a fully operational backyard greenhouse setup, covering layout decisions, equipment choices, and what's actually growing — useful if you're in the planning or early-build phase yourself. The channel's strength is showing real trial-and-error rather than a finished, perfect system, which makes the advice more transferable. Skip it if you're not actively thinking about a greenhouse; bookmark it if you are.

items.title: bandgap reference - voltage reference - voltage source - start-up circuit
items.description:
This video talks about Bandgap reference. Voltage references, independent from temperature, process and supply are very important in electronics. The bandgap reference is a good way to produce voltage references with a very little temperature dependence and therefore also a very little process dependence. 

Wilson current mirror: https://youtu.be/iMaGTSAGVmo

Bibliography : Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits by Behzad Razavi
items.why_watch: A compact, technically solid walkthrough of bandgap voltage references — the circuit building block that produces stable voltage independent of temperature and supply variation — including the start-up circuit problem that textbooks often gloss over. It assumes you know what a current mirror is (there's a linked prerequisite video) but doesn't pad the runtime with unnecessary background. Electronics students or hobbyists moving into analog IC design will find this more useful than most written explanations.

morning_soundtrack.title: Mon Laferte: Tiny Desk Concert
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Mon Laferte aims to contradict, expose or challenge norms; she takes the assignment of performing in an office space as no exception.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The electric thrill of watching someone refuse to be contained by a room that was never meant to hold them.

morning_soundtrack.title: Watch the 2026 AmericanaFest Day Stage live
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Watch live performances from the AmericanaFest Day Stage, showcasing the best of Americana, folk and blues.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Dusty boots, cold beer, and the kind of afternoon that stretches out like a country road with no end in sight.

morning_soundtrack.title: Watch the 2026 Americana Honors & Awards
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Each year, the Americana Music Association honors distinguished members of the music community.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The warm, tearful pride of watching your people get their flowers in a room full of believers.

morning_soundtrack.title: Bob Dylan Announces 39-CD Rolling Thunder Revue Box Set With 371 Previously Unreleased Tracks
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Earlier this year, Bob Dylan embarked on a US tour , surprising fans with deep cuts and new touring band members . Now, the legendary musician is announcing a 39-CD box set called The Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings , and it has 371 previously unreleased tracks.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like discovering a locked room in a house you thought you knew, stuffed floor to ceiling with someone else's memories of 1976.

morning_soundtrack.title: Wednesday Announce Deluxe Bleeds With Demos, Remixes, & Covers
morning_soundtrack.snippet: A year ago this week, Wednesday released Bleeds , an incendiary album that continued their yearslong hot streak and ranks among 2025's masterpieces . To mark the one-year anniversary, the trendsetting North Carolina rockers are releasing a deluxe edition of the album this Friday padded out with demos, remixes, and covers.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Cracking open something you loved and finding it's even rawer and more wounded at the seams.

morning_soundtrack.title: FFO: Chillin – “Perpetual Motion”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Concord, New Hampshire band FFO: Chillin has a warm, comforting, instantly familiar sound that's weirdly hard to describe. They basically make big, hearty '90s-style indie-punk anthems with occasional hardcore breakdowns, and their songs tend to be really short. Last month, they released " All I Know ," their first single for the great hardcore-centric label DAZE, and I saw them open for Joyce Manor and Glitterer in Charlottesville.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The sweaty, joyful catharsis of a basement show where everyone already knows every word somehow.

morning_soundtrack.title: ALBUM REVIEW: Nicole Atkins Addresses Modern Life While Honoring Her Heroes on 'Drama'
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Nicole Atkins commented recently that she strives to “write modern songs that could be part of the Great American Songbook.” Indeed, the influence of various artists from the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s can be heard throughout her oeuvre. Drama , like previous work, blends tried-and-true pop approaches
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A cocktail-hour glow with a modern ache underneath, like a vintage dress worn to a very contemporary heartbreak.

morning_soundtrack.title: SPOTLIGHT: Jude Brothers’ Kaleidoscopic Album ‘Dogwood Maiden Voyage’ Navigates Through Nature and Reinvention
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Editor's Note: Jude Brothers, whose new LP titled Dogwood Maiden Voyage is due out September 25 via Gar Hole Records, is No Depression's Spotlight Artist for September 2026. Stay tuned all month for more about this Ozarks singer-songwriter and
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Morning mist over Ozark hillsides, the kind of quiet that asks you to sit still and listen for once.

morning_soundtrack.title: Bob Dylan Somehow Finds 371 Unreleased Songs for Another Rolling Thunder Box Set
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The 39-disc Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings documents the fabled tour’s second leg
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The dizzy feeling of an archive that keeps going deeper, like a hallway that refuses to end.

morning_soundtrack.title: @ Roll Out 2027 Tour Dates and New Song
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Philadelphia psych-folk band previews Autosmile with “Bird”
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Sunlit and slightly untethered, like watching birds trace patterns only they understand.

morning_soundtrack.title: Dollar Brand/Don Cherry/Carlos Ward :: The Third World-Underground
morning_soundtrack.snippet: A live recording of three jazz masters in transitional phases of their careers, The Third World-Underground captures Abdullah Ibrahim (Dollar Brand), Don Cherry and Carlos Ward embarking on a joyous, lyrical and profoundly stomping set of tunes, teeming with fanfares, shouts and unruly dances. Newly reissued and remastered, this once Japanese-only release is ready to find its rightful audience. Where Ibrahim, Cherry and Ward are going, they don't need bass or drums.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Three visionaries chasing each other through open space, no map, no safety net, pure joyous flight.

morning_soundtrack.title: Wendy & Bonnie :: Genesis
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Stunning psychedelic baroque pop meets Latin-influenced west coast jazz. The story of teenage sisters Wendy & Bonnie and their sublime 1969 record Genesis is one for the books, recorded on the Skye label of family friend and vibraphone extraordinaire Cal Tjader and Gábor Szabó. Brimming with gusto and the sisters' youthful ambition yet confident and chilling sunshine pop harmonies, the duo's lone album is a maturely stunning accomplishment on several fronts.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Summer through a prism — teenage, golden, impossibly self-assured, gone too soon.

global_silver_linings.title: $1,000 Bonus for Every Year at the Company: Casino Employees Shocked at Company’s 50th Anniversary
global_silver_linings.snippet: When thousands of employees at Station Casinos arrived at one of the company’s resorts to celebrate its 50th anniversary, they hadn’t a clue what was about to happen. They were going to hit the jackpot. In a stunning display of profit sharing, business moguls the Fertitta brothers announced that each of Station Casinos’ 10,000 employees […]
global_silver_linings.reason: In an era of stagnant wages and disposable workforces, one company chose to genuinely reward loyalty — a reminder that some employers still see their people as worth celebrating. It's a small but real sign that generosity in the workplace isn't extinct.

global_silver_linings.title: ‘Would you let your child wear this?’: Mom asks if she’s ‘overreacting’ to a Target dress.
global_silver_linings.snippet: "I don’t usually even let my girls wear bikinis, but maybe I’m overreacting, I don’t know. Thoughts?”
global_silver_linings.reason: A mom questioning what's appropriate for her child is a completely ordinary act of parenting — and the fact that these conversations happen openly means families are still thinking carefully about the world they're raising kids in.

global_silver_linings.title: The Mercator map has distorted Africa’s size for 450 years. The UN just voted to replace it.
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM On most world maps hanging in classrooms, conference rooms, and government offices around the world, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size. The reality is that they are not. Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers while Africa covers 30.4 million.
global_silver_linings.reason: For 450 years, a flawed map quietly shrank an entire continent in the global imagination — and now that's being corrected, a meaningful step toward seeing the world, and each other, more honestly.

discovery_articles.title: The Adam and Eve House in Nice, France
discovery_articles.snippet: Located at 8 rue Poissonnerie, this ancient house is famous for its impressive façade dating back to 1584. This makes it one of the last remaining examples of such a painted house from that period left in the city. The facade was decorated using "sgraffito" a technique popular in Italy during the 15th and 16th centuries.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Sgraffito — the art of scratching through wet plaster to reveal a contrasting layer beneath — gives this 1584 façade a ghostly, layered quality that most of Nice has long since painted over or torn down. It's a survival as much as it is a decoration.

discovery_articles.title: The Mountain House in Woodside, California
discovery_articles.snippet: The Mountain House isn't just a restaurant; it's a dining experience tucked among the redwoods of Kings Mountain in Woodside California. A winding mountain road must be traveled to reach the destination nestled beneath some of California's tallest trees. The rustic cabin feels storybook-like, as if it were built for a family of gnomes rather than hungry diners.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: There's something quietly radical about a restaurant that requires a winding mountain pilgrimage through old-growth redwoods just to earn your dinner. The journey is the reservation.

discovery_articles.title: Larz Anderson Auto Museum in Brookline, Massachusetts
discovery_articles.snippet: Located slightly northwest of Harvard's Arnold Arboretum and within a residential area is Larz Anderson Park. A relatively small park compared to others in the area, but within this park contains a grand carriage house built during the Victorian era and housed within is the oldest automotive collection in the United States dating back to before the 20th century. The park and the auto museum are named after French born American diplomat Larz Anderson.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A Victorian carriage house quietly holding America's oldest automotive collection feels like the perfect metaphor for how quickly one era swallows the last — horses out, horseless carriages in, all under the same grand roof.

discovery_articles.title: Renovations at Buckingham Palace Have Revealed Fascinating Artifacts Previously Lost to Time Lodged in Its Walls and Floors
discovery_articles.snippet: The findings include a card game tournament ticket, an important newspaper clipping and the schedule for a diplomatic evening event under Elizabeth II
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The walls of Buckingham Palace have been keeping secrets the way all grand old houses do — tucked between the plaster, a card tournament ticket and a diplomatic schedule serve as tiny, accidental time capsules of ordinary life inside an extraordinary address.

discovery_articles.title: What If Emmett Till Had Lived? A New Exhibition Imagines an Alternate Future for the Murdered Black Teenager
discovery_articles.snippet: Featuring photographs by more than 110 artists, the show honors Till’s memory by inviting viewers to contemplate the person he might have become had he made it to adulthood
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Rather than memorializing Emmett Till solely through grief, this exhibition takes the rarer, more tender approach: imagining the full life that was stolen, which somehow makes the loss land harder, not lighter.

discovery_articles.title: These Four Giant Dinosaur Footprints Discovered in North Dakota Might Represent the First Trackway Made by an Adult T. Rex Ever Found
discovery_articles.snippet: A high school teacher first spotted the remarkable trail while volunteering on a paleontological dig. Researchers suspect a hulking, full-grown dinosaur marched through the then-swampy landscape roughly 66.5 million years ago
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A high school teacher volunteering on a dig spotted what researchers believe may be the first confirmed adult T. rex trackway ever found — proof that the most astonishing discoveries still sometimes belong to the careful, unhurried eye.

discovery_articles.title: Six Ways That People of the Past Used Magic to Protect Their Homes, From Witch Bottles to Mystical Symbols
discovery_articles.snippet: Throughout history, humans around the world have employed protective talismans such as special stones, herbs and plants, and decorative demon tiles
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The witch bottle — a sealed vessel packed with bent nails, hair, and urine buried beneath a threshold — was essentially our ancestors' home security system, and archaeologists keep finding them, still intact, still waiting.

discovery_articles.title: Meet Swiftiephylus, an Australian bug named after Taylor Swift
discovery_articles.snippet: Four newly described species of Australian plant bug have been named in honor of renowned recording artist Taylor Swift.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Taxonomy's greatest flex: a tiny Australian plant bug will now carry Taylor Swift's name in the scientific record long after the tour merch has faded. *Swiftiephylus* is, arguably, the most permanent fan tribute in existence.

discovery_articles.title: ‘Bogland’ explores beautifully strange ecosystems
discovery_articles.snippet: Ecologist Merritt Turetsky’s devotion to bogs, fens and other fascinating water-logged spaces saturates her new book.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Bogs are one of the planet's most underestimated ecosystems — quietly storing more carbon than all the world's forests combined — and Merritt Turetsky has spent her career waist-deep in their cold, peculiar wonder trying to get the rest of us to care.

discovery_articles.title: It’s “A Cat-astrophe”! (1919)
discovery_articles.snippet: “A Cat-astrophe” came on the tail end of an odd 1918 boom in cat-themed music.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The fact that 1918 — a year of pandemic and war — somehow produced a boom in whimsical cat-themed music says something deeply human about us: when the world goes dark, we reach for the absurd and the soft.

discovery_articles.title: How Cambodian Pop Music Survived the Khmer Rouge
discovery_articles.snippet: After genocide decimated the country’s musicians, old recordings helped a new generation reconnect with Cambodia’s musical past.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The Khmer Rouge systematically targeted musicians as symbols of a culture they wanted erased, yet old vinyl records survived in hiding and diaspora collections — making Cambodian pop music's revival an act of cultural resurrection as much as nostalgia.

discovery_articles.title: How Monumental Environmental Works by Meg Webster Cultivate Reconnection
discovery_articles.snippet: Inside Webster's interdisciplinary practice that advocates for nature.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Meg Webster's work asks a quietly subversive question: what if monumental art didn't dominate a landscape but tended to it instead, becoming less sculpture and more stewardship?

discovery_articles.title: Art History and Pop Culture Converge in Friedrich Kunath’s ‘The Nearest Faraway Place’
discovery_articles.snippet: The artist describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.”
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Wanting a painting to feel like a song is one of those deceptively simple ambitions that takes an entire career to even approach — Friedrich Kunath seems to be getting somewhere close.

featured_read.title: What Trump’s Bizarre Posts Are Teaching Us About AI
featured_read.snippet: The president’s recent Truth Social barrage of fake images reflects the dangers—for all of us—of virtual self-aggrandizement.
featured_read.blurb: When a sitting president floods his feed with AI-generated self-mythology, something stranger than propaganda is happening — this piece asks what it reveals about the human hunger to rewrite oneself into legend. A quiet, unsettling read about power, image, and the stories we let machines tell for us.

reading_room.title: Shall We Play a Game?
reading_room.snippet: Historian Jon Peterson traces the route from Prussian military headquarters to Gary Gygax’s basement.
reading_room.blurb: The wargame that shaped modern tabletop gaming began not in a hobbyist's garage but in the Prussian military's obsession with simulating death — Jon Peterson traces that unlikely genealogy with the precision of a historian and the delight of someone who clearly loves a good dungeon.

reading_room.title: Chasing la dolce vita
reading_room.snippet: Homecomings, fantasies, food and ghosts – how the myth of eternal return keeps the Italian diaspora in a state of longing - by Ben Faccini Read on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: Ben Faccini explores the particular ache of the Italian diaspora: the way an imagined homeland — built from Sunday ragù and half-remembered summers — becomes more vivid, and more tyrannical, than the place itself ever was. A meditation on longing that will find you wherever you are.

reading_room.title: Mercury Has Gotten Smaller Than We Thought
reading_room.snippet: The first planet from the sun has been hiding its wrinkles
reading_room.blurb: Mercury has been quietly shrinking for billions of years, its wrinkled surface a planetary diary of cooling and contraction — and scientists just realized they've been underreading it. A small story about a small planet that opens into something vast.

reading_room.title: Say yes to regret
reading_room.snippet: After my husband died, I fell into a dark ruminative spiral. The way back would begin at 2pm tomorrow - by Sandra Lamb Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Sandra Lamb writes about grief's cruellest trick: the ruminative spiral that masquerades as loyalty to the person you've lost, and the counterintuitive therapy — scheduling regret for 2pm — that began to loosen its grip. Precise, hard-won, and genuinely useful.

reading_room.title: You Have to Ask Questions: Svetlana Alexievich, Unlocked
reading_room.snippet: This week, we’ve unlocked “Voices from Chernobyl” from the archive.
reading_room.blurb: Svetlana Alexievich built *Voices from Chernobyl* from the testimonies of the forgotten — liquidators, widows, children who touched the reactor's glow — and The Paris Review has unlocked this conversation with her about why bearing witness demands you ask questions even when answers are impossible. Set aside the half-hour; it earns it.

garden_note.note: September is doing its quiet, golden work in Zürich tonight — the lindens have finished their summer story and the first leaves on the Zürichberg are just beginning to turn amber at the edges. Step outside after supper; the air already carries that particular cool that reminds you autumn is not a metaphor.

fern_data.top_pick_title: The Shape of Things We Inherited
